🇺🇸 US retailers: Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Best Buy - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- 🇬🇧 UK retailers: Amazon - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock Smyths Toys - Switch 2 console: check stock - Switch 2 Pro controller: check stock ---------------------------------- Latest LIVE updates
It's a big day for Zelda fans. Today (Nov. 5) sees the launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and retailers could mark the occasion with a restock of the limited-edition Zelda-themed Nintendo Switch 2 console and matching Zelda-themed Pro controller. And I'm tracking stock now.
Anything Zelda-related will sell out fast, and since this console was revealed and pre-orders went live in early September, it's been very tough to find in stock. But Nintendo has promised more is on the way, and Ocarina of Time launch day seems like the perfect time for more restock.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . Target, Walmart and Best Buy are all reported to have in-store drops, so check your nearest locations. Meanwhile, Target previously confirmed it will restock the Zelda Switch 2 online on Friday (Nov. 6) . Here's hoping more follow suit.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years and have helped thousands of gamers secure limited edition items during that time. Today I'm using all my experience to bring you the latest Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Switch 2 stock updates.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
I've seen a few reports indicating that Amazon is suddenly delaying Ocarina of Time pre-orders by nearly a week.
To put it mildly, people are not happy .
Did you pre-order through Amazon? Are you seeing delays on delivery? Let me know in the comments or send me an email.
Our link to the Zelda console is broken and no longer goes to a page for the special edition Switch 2.
I tried searching for the console on the Walmart and nothing shows up. I tried links on other sites which now redirect to the Ocarina of Time remake.
I'll keep an eye on things but for now Walmart has vanished the 40th anniversary console and pro controller from its website.
The console have been sold out for a minute with no real restock coming in.
I decided to check out the Pro controllers just in case any of those were available instead.
Unfortunately, I'm not seeing it available anywhere. But I'll keep looking in case it pops up.
Did you know there are two cover variants of the Ocarina of Time physical edition?
There's a textured foil version and a normal. You'll know which you have if the spine lettering is gold (foil) or white (normal).
As of this posting here is what different retailers are offering. Foil cover:
The main UK retailers have been out of stock for most of the day, but I checked again just in case anyone is trying to get one before dinner.
Of the retailers I checked, Argos might have some but you'll need to put in your postal code to check. I tried several London codes and Bradford just to see but all those locations were out of stock.
We mentioned it above but as a reminder, if Target is your preferred or closest retailer, the company does not have stock today.
However, Target previously confirmed that it will open up sales on Friday (November 6).
That being said, I found claims on Reddit that some stores were selling the consoles today. It seems like those sold out quickly though.
Nintendo is selling an official playable Ocarina from the Ocarina of Time remake for $34.99. From my understanding it actually works.
Unfortunately, it's already sold out, but I'll keep an eye on things in case it pops back up.
Stock is not lasting long. I just posted about the official Nintendo Store twenty minutes ago and the Zelda console is already sold out.
With that in mind, lets take a look at all the retailers right now.
It should be noted that GameStop is in-store only. I checked in my area and was told that no store within 100 miles had stock. You might get luckier.
Also, Walmart features third-party sellers so you might see some availability but they're also gouging the price all the way up to $700. I recommend you avoid those.
If you prefer to get your gear directly from the source, it appears that the 40th Anniversary Switch 2 is available on the official Nintendo Store.
Check out the Nintendo Switch 2 - The Legend of Zelda - 40th Anniversary Edition for $519.99 on the Nintendo store.
Hopefully you managed to secure a Zelda Pro controller if that was on your wishlist during the Walmart restock. On my end the retailer is now once again showing the dreaded "sold out" message. I'm already watching for more restocks!
Last week, Target confirmed it would restock the Zelda Switch 2 console on Friday, November 6 via an update on its listing page, before removing said update, leading to fears the restock had been delayed. Good news! The message has returned, Target will restock tomorrow (Nov. 6) , and on the same day it will also restock the console in-store. So you can try both at your nearest Target and online.
It's not the console, but you can pick up the Zelda-themed Switch 2 Pro Controller at Walmart. The page already has a "low stock" warning though, so don't expect it to stick around long. If you want this nifty Switch 2 accessory, go grab it now.
If you're in the U.K. and haven't picked up your copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time yet, you can currently grab it for £54 on Amazon . That's a £5 saving. Not a huge discount, but any form of deal on a new release is pretty rare!
Sadly, on Amazon US, the game is listed at its standard $69 MSRP . In fact, it appears Ocarina is so popular that Amazon is having stock issues, with new orders not expected to arrive until November 12-13. So you might want to get it digitally.
Still nothing new to report on the restock front, so to pass the time, let me know your favorite The Legend of Zelda game in the above poll! I'd personally pick Breath of the Wild, but there are several classic Zelda games I still need to play.
With the U.S. starting to wake up, it's worth noting that the best chance of securing a Zelda Switch 2 today appears to be in-store rather than online. We know that Target, Best Buy, Walmart and GameStop have had in-store restock, though social media suggests the majority of inventory was snapped up during various midnight launch events. However, if you live local to a retailer, and don't mind taking the chance, you'll want to head over in person and try your luck!
It's Ocarina of Time launch day. The game is in the wild, and players are taking their first steps into this visually-stunning remake. If you haven't picked up your copy yet, what are you waiting for? I'll be diving into my own just arrived copy soon, but fear not, I'm still here for several more hours tracking Switch 2 restock!

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
Authorities will be scrambling to follow any information that might lead them to a culprit
The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.
In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.
They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not  be real.
It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.
Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.
There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.
Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.
Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?
But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.
There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".
That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.
Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

articles.content_orig:

US first lady Melania Trump brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together at the White House on Thursday, calling on both sides to choose "humanity over war" ahead of talks next week in Abu Dhabi.
Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, attended the rare face-to-face gathering with Ukrainian officials. The event marked a six-day ceasefire that Melania Trump helped negotiate in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which expired on Sunday.
It came as the Trump administration is stepping up efforts to bring an end to Russia's war in Ukraine , which started when Russian troops invaded in early 2022. A trilateral meeting involving officials from the US, Ukraine, and Russia is set for November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady stated at the event. "We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people," she added.
Melania Trump said she was "involved in every stage of the planning" for the short-term ceasefire, which included reviewing aerial photos and evaluating road and hospital access.
President Trump, who did not attend, praised his wife’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire, remarking to reporters in October that "she does better than our professionals."
Dmitriev was expected to meet US officials while in Washington, according to two people familiar with his plans.
Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia and human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets also attended the gathering. They encouraged the Slovenian-born Melania Trump to maintain her peace efforts.
Both delegations presented the first lady with gifts of appreciation.
Russia’s Dmitriev presented her with a drawing of pink hearts by an Oleshky girl, stating the child "chose to live with her family in Russia," alluding to the dispute over displaced Ukrainian children in Russia. "I love Melania," the artwork stated.
The Ukrainian delegation presented the first lady with a state honor "for your brave heart, for saving our people, and for returning back Ukrainian children."
She provided the visiting delegates with letters addressed to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meeting was the first face-to-face contact between Russian and US officials following Tuesday's midterm elections, where Democrats won control of Congress from Republicans, dealing a blow to President Trump.
The incoming Democratic majority starting in January is expected to push for increased aid to Ukraine and scrutinize the Republican president's decisions to arrange a diesel deal with Russia and ease certain Moscow sanctions. Trump has heightened his criticism of Zelensky in recent weeks.
The Kremlin noted it hopes Trump will persist with his peace efforts despite the Republican Party’s loss.
It also stated preparations were under way for a summit between Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China.
Dmitriev previously met Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, at the White House in 2025. Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden, did not invite Russian representatives to the White House.
Dmitriev has assisted in facilitating the release of American detainees in Russia, reuniting Ukrainian children with their families, and supporting the humanitarian effort in Oleshky.

articles.title_orig: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.title_zh: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.content_orig:
An update has ballooned Nier: Automata’s file size to 366GB on Steam.
This is seemingly caused by a bug that has added the full game’s file size to the file size of each DLC. When stacked up, it means you will need 366GB of space to install the full game and its adds-ons, despite it only being around 50GB prior to the update being pushed out.
While initially suspected to be a typo on Steam , RPG Site has since tested this out and indeed found that Nier: Automata now requires 366GB of space. It’s likely the bug will be addressed in a hotfix soon, so it’s worth holding off on installing Nier: Automata or the new update until then. It’s also a handy reminder to switch off auto updates on Steam if you’re unable to revert back right now.
Some report that the issue is fixed on their end, but others are still showing inflated file sizes when they go to install the game or the new update. The store page still says that you just need 50GB of space to install the game. It only seems that you’ll be asked for the additional space when you actually attempt to install it after purchase.
Curiously, the update that caused this hasn’t even added much to the game, instead adding support for three new languages (Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese).
Unsurprisingly, the game is seeing some negative reviews come in, seemingly from those unable to play the game now that it wants to eat up so much space on their PCs. Right now, neither Square Enix nor Platinum Games has acknowledged the mistake, so it’s unclear when a fix will be rolled out everywhere.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.
Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla.
Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail.
“It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.”
Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit.
And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts.
SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans.
“I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose.
Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares.
The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions.
Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches.
SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year.
How AI companies spent money on the midterms
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.”
Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.)
Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country.
Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads.
Musk bankrolling group using AI to attack Talarico on AI
“It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said.
Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said.
Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: France strikes live: largest day of protests in years expected as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes live: largest day of protests in years expected as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles broke out in Nantes and authorities arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by an estimated 575,000 people – remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike was organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors were impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
At least 448 people have been detained during the nationwide protests in France, the country’s Interior Ministry said, though that is a fraction of the estimated 575,000 who took part.
The ministry revised down its count of protesters, from the 600,000 it reported earlier today .
There were about 65,000 protesters in Paris alone, the ministry said.
The marches across the country were largely peaceful and proceeded without major incidents, the ministry said. There were some clashes between police and “groups of radical and far-left activists” in places like Rennes, Nantes, Lyon and Marseille, it said.
Firefighters responded to 86 fires, including one at a school common room that was destroyed in Toulouse, it said. An effigy of a police riot officer was set on fire in Strasbourg.
Hundreds of thousands of people are protesting across France today, but it’s a movement that grew out of protests that happened two months ago.
In September, students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs went on strike, demanding more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
The movement has since swelled into a collective cry of anger, bringing together groups with different grievances, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
No longer confined to students, the movement has drawn in trade unions and yellow vest protesters, who are voicing frustrations over the cost of living and calling for French President Emmanuel Macron to go. The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions.
With so many causes now fueling the protests, the anger is unlikely to subside anytime soon.
And with France heading into a deeply divisive presidential election in April , the stakes are only getting higher.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed at the end of October that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
The skyrocketing cost of living in France is one of the factors driving this wave of protests as anxieties around low wages, high prices and the state of public services explode onto the streets.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.
In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.
The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near stands

articles.title_orig: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers
articles.title_zh: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters' view of data centers
articles.content_orig:
New commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.
The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.
The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.
Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact ⁠ (opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.
This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio , covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.
Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
Protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.
Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.
That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.
Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.
Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.
The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

Outback Steakhouse parent company Bloomin' Brands is moving to acquire 61 restaurants operated by a major franchisee that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.
Out West Restaurant Group, which operates Outback Steakhouse locations across the western United States, filed for bankruptcy protection in Delaware on Monday, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Bloomin' Brands has entered into an agreement to purchase Out West's assets for approximately $26.3 million, subject to certain adjustments and the assumption of specified liabilities.

articles.title_orig: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.title_zh: IRS announces new federal income tax brackets for 2027
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Here are the federal income tax brackets for 2027:
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia Has No Easy Choices as It Weighs How to Combat Houthi Threat
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia Has No Easy Choices as It Weighs How to Combat Houthi Threat
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s internationally recognized National Committee for Regulating and Financing Imports is tightening financial control over goods entering Houthi-controlled ports, the Aden Chamber of Commerce and Industry reported Thursday. The decision requires customs duties, taxes, and other government revenues to be paid in advance on imports destined for Houthi-controlled ports, it said.
The new measures, which were circulated earlier this week, make the processing of foreign-exchange transactions and related international transfers conditional on proof that the applicable charges have been paid in full.
Critics have warned that the requirements could create an additional financial burden for businesses importing supplies into the poverty-stricken country.
Last week, Yemeni economic journalist Wafiq Saleh told Yemen Youth TV Channel the small quantity of imports allowed to enter the besieged city of Taiz was not meeting residents’ basic needs, and that the country was falling into a war-driven economy, with inflated black-market prices for basic goods.
The Yemeni government’s new measures were “an important economic tool in the hands of the Central Bank and the National Committee for Import Financing in the face of traders and importers,” he wrote on social media.
“Traders and importers who attempt to circumvent this mechanism will find it difficult to cover letters of credit for goods imported from abroad,” Saleh wrote. “The Central Bank of Yemen in Aden is the authorized entity for covering letters of credit and communicating with regional correspondent banks and intermediary banks. No commercial or banking entity will be able to access the international financial system outside of the official monetary authorities.”
Since the Houthis captured Sanaa in 2014, the group has collected revenues through taxes, customs duties, zakat (religious alms), and other levies, the independent Yemeni research and policy institution Mokha Center for Strategic Studies reported.
The Houthis’ “parallel economy” accounted for about $2.5 billion annually in direct and indirect financial resources and costs, it reported in July.
About $800 million came from taxes and customs, $600m. from additional fees and levies, $300m. from cash and in-kind contributions to the war effort, and $100m. from mobilization events, the report said. A further $700m. represented indirect costs borne by businesses, it added.
On Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Houthis had demanded $51b. from Saudi Arabia as compensation for years of Saudi airstrikes and a prolonged blockade, alongside formal recognition of the group as Yemen’s rulers, in exchange for ending hostilities.
Saudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks by Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28.
In response, Riyadh has sought to strengthen its regional defense partnerships. In August, signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. On Wednesday, it signed a separate defense cooperation agreement with Syria.

articles.title_orig: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
articles.title_zh: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Stocks plummet as Democratic landslide adds to investors’ AI fears
U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers.
The Justice Department was ordered to respond to the allegations, made by the ship’s Russian owner, Burevestmarin LLC, by 9 a.m. Friday.
The tanker, Bella 1, was seized by the U.S. military in the North Atlantic in early January after a weekslong chase on the high seas. U.S. authorities said the ship, which they believed was carrying illegal Iranian oil, was caught fleeing an American blockade of Venezuela . Attorneys for Burevestmarin dispute the claim that the vessel was carrying Iranian oil.
The ship was sold to a scrap dealer for $9.1 million, the company’s lawyers said, well below the $21 million that the Bella 1 would fetch as scrap metal alone.
Even a proper scrap metal price tag would understate its worth, they added, because the ship has “substantially greater value” as “an operating commercial vessel.”
“As discussed and previously briefed, the Government posits a world in which it can — while withholding notice to known interested parties and while aware of challenges to the Court’s jurisdiction — engage in precisely this kind of economically irrational sale for its own convenience,”  the owner’s lawyers wrote.
They said the sale was conducted “behind closed doors” as part of the government’s “self-interested and unreasonable decisions.”
Representatives for the Justice Department and the scrap dealer named in court documents could not be immediately reached for comment Thursday.
Previously, DOJ attorneys have argued that seized ships put the government in a financial bind, so selling these vessels is necessary to avoid tens of millions of dollars in maintenance and repair costs.
DOJ attorney Rajbir Datta told the court in July that “the government has spent $60 million in maintaining this and doing all kinds of mechanical fixes to the asset itself.”
A root issue in the ongoing court battle is whether American authorities are right to argue that transporting Iranian oil benefits the sanctioned Islamic Revolutionary Guards Force.
That question is further complicated by the Trump administration permitting international sale of Iranian oil to help relieve domestic fuel prices.
Attorneys representing Bella 1’s owner are also fighting the Justice Department’s efforts to seize other ships that they own, citing what they believe is a legal double standard invoked by the government, court records show.
In the case of the vessel Galileo attorneys for the ship owner argued that “on March 20, 2026, the same day that the Government (under seal and ex parte) alleged that the Galileo was a source of influence over the IRGC and IRGC-QF, it expressly licensed the international sale of Iranian oil — an action that would be illegal under multiple statutes were the shipment of Iranian oil in itself necessarily the equivalent of providing a means of support to the IRGC or IRGC-QF or becoming the property of the IRGC or IRGC-QF.”
In the case of another vessel, Skipper, attorneys for Burevestmarin LLC said the Justice Department did not establish the correct venue and may have improperly seized that vessel. The Skipper was on the “high seas” thus meaning it was outside of the U.S. or a foreign country’s territorial waters.
Tom Winter is NBC’s National Law Enforcement and Intelligence Correspondent.

articles.title_orig: McDonald's plans new value menu offerings next year to boost sluggish sales
articles.title_zh: McDonald's plans new value menu offerings next year to boost sluggish sales
articles.content_orig:
A ‘Barron’s Roundtable' panel discusses how the fast-food chain will manage the pinch to consumers wallets.
McDonald's is testing new value menu offerings with an eye toward launching a new national value menu program in early 2027.
The fast-food giant has sought to counter slowing traffic in the U.S. as the company's quarterly earnings release on Wednesday revealed comparable sales in the U.S. declined 0.2% in the third quarter.
McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said during the company's most recent earnings call that, in the last week of October, McDonald's began an eight-week test of two new everyday affordable price menu constructs across all day parts at about 1,900 restaurants in a handful of regions.
The test involves mix-and-match bundles to give customers greater choices that are similar to prior buy one, add one offers, as well as fixed bundles with a set combination.
MCDONALD'S TO SPEND $8.5B ON REVAMPING RESTAURANTS, TECH AND FRANCHISE SUPPORT
The McDonald's CEO added that a group of franchisees representing about 4,000 restaurants are moving forward with similar entry-level bundles in advance of the formal test results. Kempczinski said the two groups together "represent more than 40% of the U.S. system, reflecting strong alignment around the opportunity."
McDonald's is planning to roll out a new value menu push early next year after it assesses the results of tests to close out this year. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"We use the results of this test to determine which structure resonates most with customers, works best operationally and delivers sustainable incremental traffic and sales for franchisees," Kempczinski said. "Our goal is to launch a new program nationally in early 2027.
"Our goal is straightforward. Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald's, whether they're looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal or a digital offer in the mobile app."
MCDONALD'S SAYS US SALES SLOWED AFTER VALUE DEAL PUSH FELL SHORT
McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company wants to provide a clear value proposition for customers considering the fast-food giant. (McDonald's Corporation)
The value menu plans come after McDonald's in September announced a multi-year plan called "NEXT" that will focus on upgrading restaurants and staff training, as well as deploying technology.
The company will spend $8.5 billion as part of the NEXT strategy through 2036, with about $5 billion of that spending provided through 2030. The NEXT partnering support for franchisees will include a combination of capital support and rent relief.
MCDONALD'S SHAKES UP FALL COFFEE LINEUP AS PUMPKIN SPICE SEASON HEATS UP
McDonald's global CFO Ian Borden said on the earnings call that the fast-food chain is already putting elements of the NEXT strategy into action, including rolling out a new beverage platform , starting the "Make It Golden" training initiative, and setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken.
Borden added that the company is starting to open remodeled NEXT restaurants around the world, including the first international restaurant in Poland.

The company will begin remodeling hundreds of U.S. restaurants in 2027 to revise kitchen layouts and equipment to support future menu changes. McDonald's aims to ramp up to a global run rate above 5,000 restaurants per year in 2028.

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump .
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war . It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
Aidan  Stretch contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices hit two-month low following decisive midterm election results
articles.title_zh: Oil prices hit two-month low following decisive midterm election results
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices jumped Thursday, as investors reassessed the outlook for ‌the US-Israeli war with Iran while new attacks on tankers fed worries about oil supplies.
Brent crude futures rose 4% to $98.44 a barrel by 2:42 p.m. ET. US West Texas Intermediate crude increased 2.9% to $90.71 a barrel.
On Wednesday, both benchmarks tumbled more than 8% to their lowest settlement levels since August 31.
"The situation in the Middle East is ​still unresolved and that's why there is some modest recovery in prices at the moment," said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at UBS.
Andy Lipow, ​president of Lipow Oil Associates, said reports of tankers striking mines in the Middle East or being targeted by drones continue ⁠to worry the oil market. Investors are also worried about Iran's unchanged position regarding negotiations with the US.
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are ​still running close to a record pace with at least five vessels having reported incidents since Sunday, according to UK maritime security agency UKMTO. The pace was ​similar to October when the agency said 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war.
The war on Iran, which US President Donald Trump launched along with Israel in February, resulted in sharply higher fuel prices, which became major grievances for voters. Democrats took control of both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, routing Trump's ​Republican Party.
The new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office in January.
Citi said in a note there were concerns that with the midterms over, the White House could ​focus on its executive powers in foreign policy and potentially escalate the war with Iran.
Eurasia Group, however, lowered its estimate for the chance of renewed US strikes on ‌Iran ⁠to 60% from 65%. It also cut the probability of a deal to 10% from 20%, as Iran has held firm on demands that Trump is viewed as unlikely to accept. Eurasia Group raised the likelihood of a continued standoff to 30% from 15%.
Despite the recent drop in oil prices, any escalation in the conflict could push Brent into a $110 to $125 per barrel range, Eurasia Group said in a note.
Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi discussed the "latest progress" in diplomatic efforts to ​promote regional stability in separate calls ​with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts, the ⁠Iranian foreign ministry said.
Tensions in the region remain elevated. Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the kingdom's Red Sea oil export hub, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis continued attacks on the kingdom ​in another front of the Iran war.
The Houthis later said they attacked King Fahd airport in the Saudi city of Dammam, although ​there was no immediate ⁠confirmation from Saudi authorities.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents after attempting to use unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Elsewhere, Ukraine renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries, raising concerns about Russia's ability to export diesel under a deal with Trump.
The Ryazan oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, ⁠appeared to ​have been targeted in a large overnight drone attack on industrial sites southeast of Moscow, ​according to a Reuters video analysis.
If confirmed, it would be the second Russian refinery hit this week, following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant on Monday night.

articles.title_orig: Bloody fight erupts over line cutters in packed tourist hotspot
articles.title_zh: Bloody fight erupts over line cutters in packed tourist hotspot
articles.content_orig:
A couple appeared to be left bloodied after a row with elderly visitors erupted into a violent confrontation at a tourist hotspot in China.
The pair reportedly became involved in an argument with a 62-year-old man and a 58-year-old woman at the Five-Coloured Pond viewing platform in Jiuzhaigou Scenic Area, Sichuan, on November 2.
Dramatic footage shows a man wearing a blue jacket repeatedly punching another man dressed in a purple top during the heated altercation.
Another clip shows the younger couple with blood covering their faces as fellow visitors gather around to help.
The dispute allegedly began when the older pair attempted to jump the queue while taking photographs at the popular viewing spot.
The younger couple reportedly challenged them over cutting in line , sparking an argument that eventually turned physical.
The pair and one of the older visitors sustained injuries during the chaos. All three received medical treatment and were later confirmed to be out of danger.
Both parties were taken to a police station for investigation and later agreed to mediation.
Officers said those involved acknowledged their mistakes, apologized to each other and reached an agreement following discussions.
Authorities urged visitors to remain calm, communicate politely and avoid allowing disagreements to escalate into violence.

articles.title_orig: Avigdor Liberman drops veto on haredi parties in coalition, opposition in talks with UTJ
articles.title_zh: Avigdor Liberman drops veto on haredi parties in coalition, opposition in talks with UTJ
articles.content_orig:
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman has dropped his veto on forming a government with haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, opening the door for the opposition bloc to begin discussions with United Torah Judaism (UTJ), N12's Amit Segal reported on Thursday
The bloc is reportedly discussing the possibility of drafting a more lenient military conscription law, and the current assumption is that Shas would be forced to support the move as well, under pressure from Rabbi Lando.
UTJ , a longtime coalition partner of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , declined to recommend a candidate for prime minister to President Isaac Herzog during the party's consultation earlier on Thursday.
UTJ's decision to abstain came amid reported tensions between the haredi party and Netanyahu, and it benefits the opposition bloc seeking to replace him. Opposition party leaders have recently signaled greater openness to including haredi parties in their coalition.
A potential coalition led by Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot and including United Torah Judaism (UTJ) would hold 55 seats in the Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority needed to form a government. However, it would reduce Netanyahu's bloc to just 46 seats, potentially allowing Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am and the Joint List abstaining.
Yisrael Beytenu denied the report in a statement to The Jerusalem Post .
"We are not aware of any such thing. Nothing has changed since the briefing was given," the party stated.
During the Monday briefing, Liberman ruled out joining a unity government with Netanayhu, along with the option of a minority government that would be reliant on support from the Arab parties. However, his stance regarding joining a coalition with  Shas and UTJ appeared to be more lenient.
Liberman stated that whoever would accept his set of principles and a conscription law to draft the haredim, he would "have no problem with."
Liberman has repeatedly ruled out joining a government with haredi parties in recent years, citing fundamental disagreements over military conscription and issues related to religion and state. He has previously declared that Yisrael Beytenu would not sit with either Arab or haredi parties, describing them as "non-Zionist elements" and arguing that anyone who refuses military service should be considered an evader.
His opposition to compromising on haredi conscription has also shaped coalition negotiations, most notably in 2019, when his refusal to support a compromise on a military draft law helped derail Netanyahu's efforts to form a government, triggering a political deadlock that led to five elections being held between 2019 and 2022.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street fear gauge jumps most since 'Liberation Day' as AI trade stumbles
articles.title_zh: Wall Street fear gauge jumps most since 'Liberation Day' as AI trade stumbles
articles.content_orig:
Whether it's a referendum on the midterms or just a continuation of a bear market in semiconductors that dates back to the group's peak in June, one thing's clear from the options action Thursday: few traders saw this coming.
That's evident in the surge in Cboe Volatility index (VIX) , which jumped as much as 5.7 points to above 28 about 90 minutes after the opening bell on Thursday. It's the highest reading on VIX since March 31, the day after the S&P 500 bottomed after selling off as tensions between Iran, Israel and the U.S. reached fever pitch.
From its intraday low to high Thursday, VIX moved more than 11 points, the biggest one-day move since April 9. Yet with the S&P 500 down 3%, there's an argument to be made that volatility should be higher. Traders use a rule of thumb that 16 points for the VIX equate to a 1% move in the index.
The S&P 500 was headed for its worst decline since April 2025.
"My data says to de-risk, but my gut says this is a blowout that could create a dip-buying opportunity" said Noel Smith, "I do not see macro stuff causing this, like oil or rates. Those things are relatively unchanged. The tape looks like a liquidation and that's exactly what it is according to what I'm hearing with regards to a hedge fund."
Looking at Wednesday's response to the selloff in semiconductors adds a wrinkle for traders that pointed to a too-calm VIX despite Wednesday's tech-stock wreck. With the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 3%, it was the first day in market history that the VIX concurrently fell more than 4 points, according to data from the X account "OddStats." As of midday, nearly 800,000 calls traded on the VIX, 3.5 times higher than 30-day average, according to Cboe data.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank, which Paraguay's central bank seized amid a solvency crisis, in Asunción, Paraguay, Wednesday. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.
The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.
Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.
Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.
Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. Ted Shaffrey/AP hide caption
As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.
Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.
"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.
Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.
On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.
Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.
Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.
"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.
The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.
Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.
The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. Across
