articles.title_orig: 2 arrested after mushroom gummies given to children on Halloween in Ocean Beach
articles.title_zh: 2 arrested after mushroom gummies given to children on Halloween in Ocean Beach
articles.content_orig:
An 80-year-old man and a 45-year-old man suspected of distributing psilocybin gummies to at least 15 trick-or-treating children in Sunset Cliffs were arrested.
An 80-year-old man and a 45-year-old man suspected of distributing psilocybin gummies, also known as "magic mushrooms" to at least 15 trick-or-treating children in Ocean Beach were taken into custody Wednesday after a a search warrant was served on the home suspected of distributing the psychedelics.
Michael Goff, 80, and Shawn Michael Foster were arrested and booked into the San Diego County Jail. Goff was booked on suspicion of possessing a firearm as a convicted felon, while Foster faces suspicion of possessing both a firearm and ammunition as a convicted felon.
Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7.
No charges were filed in connection with psilocybin-infused gummies but San Diego police said officers discovered an identical bag of psilocybin gummies to those distributed on Halloween in the home during a Wednesday morning search of the home on 2100 block of Sunset Cliffs Boulevard.
Multiple bags of psilocybin-infused gummies were left on a residence's porch Saturday night and were later taken by children between 1 and 6 years old, according to the San Diego Police Department.
Police said the children's parents noticed the suspicious candy packages and, upon inspecting them, suspected they contained controlled substances.
Frank Cary and Cameron Hunter were trick-or-treating with their children and several neighborhood families Saturday night when they made the discovery their children had obtained illicit drugs .
The parents said they were walking just a few yards behind their children when the kids approached a porch with a bowl of what appeared to be candy.
"My 2-year-old went up and grabbed one and started walking away with it in his hand,” Cary told NBC 7. “I noticed the picture had a giraffe and words that looked like they were melting. I took it out of his hand and saw that there was a dosage on the front of it. Five grams, [then I ] flipped it around and read 'psilocybin mushrooms.'”
The parents then confronted the homeowners and later filed a police report with the department, saving the packages of the gummies for law enforcement evaluation, which later tested positive for psilocybin.
NBC 7 San Diego visited the house on Monday and spoke to a man who claimed he lived at the house . The man,  who identified himself as Shawn Barger, disputed the parents' account of the situation. He said his wife had been confused when strangers came to their door and confronted her about the packages.
After the search warrant was served, detectives seized over 2.5 pounds of cannabis, more than 25 grams of crystal methamphetamine, a working digital scale, packaging materials and drug sales ledgers.
An illegally possessed rifle was also located at the residence, along with dozens of rounds of unfired ammunition and a partially assembled pistol.
According to police, a San Diego code compliance investigator responded to the scene to begin a separate investigation into the property's unpermitted living structures.
Anyone with information about the case was urged to contact the Narcotics Unit at 619-531-2468. Tipsters who prefer to remain anonymous can call Crime Stoppers at 888-580-8477.
City News Service contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China and the Netherlands Discuss Plant Breeders’ Rights, AI and Robotics
articles.title_zh: China and the Netherlands Discuss Plant Breeders’ Rights, AI and Robotics
articles.content_orig:
Protecting new plant varieties and applying artificial intelligence and robotics were central to discussions between Chinese and Dutch industry representatives at the 24th China Kunming International Flower Expo.
Organised by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in China, the dialogues brought together more than 130 breeding experts, business leaders and intellectual property professionals from China, the Netherlands and other countries.
Participants examined policy, breeding technology, judicial protection, financial implications and commercial implementation, with variety rights emerging as a key consideration for breeders entering international markets, according to a press release.
Tsjeard Hoekstra, deputy ambassador at the Dutch embassy in China, emphasised that an internationally aligned variety rights system is a prerequisite for breeders to bring their best varieties to market.
Dutch experts outlined developments in their country’s variety rights protection and regulatory approach. Discussions also highlighted that responsibility for protecting varieties extends beyond breeders to businesses involved in sales and distribution.
Li Shenchong, director of the Flower Research Institute at the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, called for greater respect for breeding innovation, standardised variety trading, stronger protection of breeding achievements and deeper cooperation. These priorities form part of China’s Initiative on Innovation and Protection of New Plant Varieties (Flowers).
For breeders navigating the lengthy process from initial selection to commercial launch, a stable protection system helps create the conditions needed to introduce new varieties.
A separate discussion explored the application of AI and robotics in floriculture, with Chinese and Dutch experts sharing practical experience with AI crop models.
Limited land availability has helped drive the Netherlands’ investment in efficient cultivation. Over decades, Dutch greenhouse technology has combined sensors, algorithms and growing expertise to reduce inputs and increase output. AI and robotic systems could accelerate that progress.
Erik Smidt, counsellor for agriculture, fisheries, food security and nature at the Dutch embassy in China, emphasised the importance of trusted partners when doing business in China.
He pointed to more than two decades of cooperation between Dutch and Chinese floriculture businesses as a foundation for combining cultivation expertise with emerging technologies.
Across both discussions, participants identified cooperation as essential to advancing the flower sector, through stronger protection for breeding innovations and technologies that help growers produce more efficiently.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Is Below $200. What History Suggests Is the Floor.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Below $200. What History Suggests Is the Floor.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.
Thursday did a lot of the damage . At the lows of the session, Nvidia was down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a matter of hours and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. A close there would be the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.
Nvidia has plenty of company.
AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) are posting steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) are falling by about 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is now more than a third below its June record. Sandisk ( SNDK ) dropped 19%.
Nvidia itself is down nearly 25% from its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .
The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.
Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.
The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.
That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.
For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.
"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

articles.title_orig: Musk has little to show for his record spending on Republican campaigns in US midterms
articles.title_zh: Musk has little to show for his record spending on Republican campaigns in US midterms
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.
Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla.
Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail.
“It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.”
Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit.
And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts.
The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans.
“I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose.
Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares.
How AI companies spent money on the midterms
The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions.
Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches.
SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year.
Musk bankrolling group using AI to attack Talarico on AI
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.”
Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.)
Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country.
Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads.
“It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said.
Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said.
Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

articles.title_orig: Why the midterm blue wave just triggered a red Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Why the midterm blue wave just triggered a red Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Tech firms tumbled on Thursday as investors contemplated the outlook for the AI boom after Democrats swept the US midterms, partly on the back of growing anger over the rapid building of data centres across the country.
However, broader markets mostly rallied and oil plunged after President Donald Trump's Republicans were dealt a historic defeat that was blamed on high prices, tariffs and the Iran war.
The result stoked hopes he will look to wind down the Middle East conflict, which would help temper inflation and even soften his stance on trade.
But AI-linked firms came under the cosh amid fears for planned data centre construction projects as well as renewed scrutiny from newly installed Democrats on Capitol Hill.
The sector had already been in the crosshairs of investors owing to questions about the vast sums pumped into new facilities, R&D and chip development, and when any companies would see a profit.
Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets said the vote was accelerating a reassessment of AI that was already under way.
"A Democratic Congress introduces another layer of uncertainty: regulatory scrutiny," she wrote, adding that the three main risks were more oversight, data centre restrictions and capital spending uncertainty.
"The congressional scrutiny could accelerate demands for AI safety standards, independent model evaluations and greater accountability for data centre developers," she added.
However, she also said: "This is not the same as an outright anti-AI policy agenda. AI is strategically important for US competitiveness, particularly against China, and there remains considerable bipartisan interest in maintaining American leadership."
Chip firms were hammered in Asia, with South Korea's SK hynix off more than 7% and Samsung 5.5% down.
Tokyo-listed Kioxia dived more than 13% and Advantest tanked 14.7%, while Tokyo Electron lost more than 9% and SoftBank 6.8%.
US Nasdaq futures fell more than 1%.
Broader markets performed better as investors rotated into other sectors including finance, auto, mining and manufacturing names.
Seoul, the poster child of the AI-led surge in the first half of the year, shed more than 5%, while Taipei lost more than 3%. Tokyo gave up 1.8%.
But there were healthy gains in Hong Kong, helped by hopes for an easing of trade tensions between the US and China, with tech titans including Alibaba, JD.com and Tencent leading the way amid a shift into beaten-down regional stocks.
Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Mumbai, Jakarta and Manila also advanced.
London, Paris and Frankfurt opened higher to extend Wednesday's spike.
Oil held losses after diving more than 8% Wednesday on the US result amid optimism Trump will seek a deal to end the Iran war, which has been a key driver of the inflation spike that has hammered US consumers.
Hopes received a boost when US Vice President JD Vance said in a social media post that the Republican defeat was due to the unpopularity of the eight-month-old conflict.
The drop in crude prices - both main contracts are now below $100 for the first time since the start of October - has also tempered inflation worries and, in turn, Treasury yields, which dipped again Thursday.
The lower cost of borrowing has also been helped by the prospect that gridlock on Capitol Hill would lead to less spending.
That also weighed on the dollar, which held losses against its peers in Asian trade.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Memecoin Sinks to All-Time Low
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Memecoin Sinks to All-Time Low
articles.content_orig:
Trump Media stock and WLFI coin saw declines but he is still $2.7bn wealthier than when he won election in 2024
US midterms 2026 live – latest updates
Send us your questions about the midterm results
Track live results from all 50 states
Donald Trump ’s wealth is falling along with his political fortunes.
Tradable investment assets that helped make the president more than $2bn during his first year in office are collapsing in value the day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections . Trump Media and Technology Group stock, which trades on the Nasdaq exchange, was priced at just over $5 on Wednesday morning – its lowest mark ever, and down from an all-time high of $101. It lost 11% overnight, dropping from $5.90 once the election returns started coming in. Trump has reported he owns 114m shares of DJT.
Trump owns over 40% of the stock through a trust. He has still grown his wealth dramatically during his presidency; Forbes estimated in a September analysis that he is $ 2.7bn wealthier than when he won the White House in 2024.
Another major asset for Trump and his family are World Liberty Financial digital tokens . The digital coins are trading at less than 5 cents after the election. At their height, in 2025, they were valued at six times that, at 31 cents. The WLFI coin, the governance token of World Liberty financial, began sliding in late October as the election drew near, and as a hack of Binance rattled crypto markets. It experienced a steep decline around 7pm ET on Tuesday as polls in some states closed.
Trump already made more than $500m in profit selling crypto assets last year, according to his personal financial disclosures, though he still owns 15bn tokens.
World Liberty is a venture created by the Trump family and the family of Steven Witkoff. Trump appointed Witkoff, a personal friend and real estate developer, to negotiate diplomatic arrangements about Gaza, Iran and Ukraine.
The value of both WLIF and DJT has always been pegged to the way Trump is perceived, said Jim Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business.
“People think they’re investing in Trump. They really aren’t. They’re really betting on his popularity. That’s what they’re betting on.
“Right now his popularity is at record lows,” Angel added, “and so we see the price of DJT and World Liberty at record lows.”
Separate digital novelty coins called $Trump , which made the president $636m in sales in 2025, have also collapsed in value. They are priced at about $1.40 and seem to have lost about 10% of their value overnight as election results came in. They launched shortly before his inauguration and briefly traded as high as $45 in January 2025.
World Liberty Financial, the Trump and Witkoff crypto company, also issues a so-called stablecoin, USDI1, and the Trump administration recently gave the company a banking license. The stablecoins are pegged to the US dollar and do not fluctuate dramatically.

articles.title_orig: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
articles.title_zh: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
articles.content_orig:
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: More ships attacked in Persian Gulf, oil prices rebound slightly after post-midterm plunge
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: More ships attacked in Persian Gulf, oil prices rebound slightly after post-midterm plunge
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin received Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between their two countries, including a pipeline to import Russian gas.
Speaking to journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent much of the day on calls with his counterparts from several Middle Eastern countries, including Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey.
In total, Araghchi held calls with nine different countries in the Middle East. Few details were shared about what was discussed on the calls, simply nodding to "diplomatic efforts to maintain stability in the region."
Notably, Pakistan was one of those countries involved as they have been very closely involved as mediators in U.S.-Iran peace talks. Araghchi spoke to their foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, on Thursday evening.
Araghchi also spoke to Saudi foreign ministers Faisal bin Farhan and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, despite accusations of Iranian involvement in attacks on that country by the Houthi militia in Yemen.
President Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."
"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."
"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis took credit for disrupting travel using a drone at King Fahd International Airport on Thursday.
"We targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam using a drone and our operation caused a disruption of air navigation at the airport," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.
The city of Dammam, which is located in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia, and King Fahd airport have been regular targets for Houthi attacks. Multiple drones have disrupted traffic at the airport this week, according to past announcements.
Two people were killed in a Houthi strike on King Fahd airport on Oct. 22.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its associated strike group will make a port call in Singapore Friday and will not reach the Middle East for at least another two weeks, a U.S. official told CBS News on Thursday.
There are already two carrier strike groups in the region and, which officials say is sufficient firepower to execute any commands issued by President Trump.
Mr. Trump has not signaled yet, in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, whether he intends to order major new strikes on Iran — an option he kept on the table with repeated statements ahead of Tuesday's voting.
The initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit Thursday.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, considered the international standard, rose 2.2% to $96.70, recovering a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before.
Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Thursday in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a message from Iran's supreme leader, according to the Iranian government.
They met amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move on Iran in the wake of U.S. midterm election results that represented a major rebuke of his policies, including, he has admitted, the decision to launch the war with Iran alongside Israel more than eight months ago.
Mr. Trump said repeatedly ahead of the Tuesday vote that he had yet to make a decision on whether to order major new attacks on Iran or to agree a deal to end the war, which Tehran has so far refused to do until the U.S. accepts its core demands to end its naval blockade, ensure a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, and ease sanctions.
During the Rezaei-Putin meeting in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned Russian citizens against all travel to Iran.
"Given the continued risk of a new escalation around Iran, our recommendations to Russian citizens remain unchanged," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters in Moscow. "We recommend temporarily refraining from traveling to that country until the situation is resolved. We also ask our compatriots already in Iran to exercise vigilance and avoid crowds, public events, and areas near military and government facilities."
She said the guidance was "based on the official information disseminated by Tehran," without providing any further detail.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry renewed the regime's rejection on Thursday of longtime and widely held beliefs that Tehran materially supports the Houthi rebels fighting the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen's decade-long civil war. The conflict intensified a couple months ago and quickly became the most active and deadly front in the intertwined conflicts in the Middle East.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the latest accusation of Iranian support for the Houthis, made Monday by European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, "baseless," and said Iran "strongly denied claims that Iranian military experts were present in Yemen."
The U.S. government, along with many other Western nations and the NATO alliance , have demanded for years that Iran stop supporting the Houthis. The support, according to these nations, includes financial backing, weapons and other equipment, and direct coordination and training.

articles.content_orig:

Bomb threats across Europe have grounded flights across several countries and caused travel disruptions on Thursday.
It marks the second time this week that such widespread threats have been reported prompting fear and concern against the backdrop of a series of cyber-attacks affecting supermarket fridges and blood banks across the continent.
Flights flying to and from the UK , Belgium , Ireland, Italy , Finland , Bulgaria , Spain and Denmark were impacted and were largely resolved by the end of the day.
More than a dozen flights were targeted, included those from Copenhagen , Dublin , Helsinki , Madrid, Milan and Warsaw.
A Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by Italian Air Force jets. A Ryanair aircraft landed at Sofia airport after planes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed in the Bulgarian capital, according to the country’s interior minister.
Inspections of three Ryanair aircraft that received bomb threats and landed at the Bulgarian airports did not identify any issues, the country’s transport ministry said.
“Upon landing, the necessary inspections were carried out in accordance with the applicable procedures and no issues were identified,” the country’s transport ministry told Reuters. Airport operations at both Sofia and Plovdiv airports have returned to normal, it said.
Airports in the UK were also impacted amid threats reported at Heathrow and Birmingham airports.
“Threats reported at Heathrow and Birmingham in the early hours of this morning have been resolved,” a government spokesperson said in a statement issued on Thursday.
“It’s right that authorities treat any potential threats seriously — the UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any threats, as well as malicious hoaxes, like those we’ve seen this week.”
The Times reported that the Metropolitan Police are continuing to monitor the situation.
Finnair also said that its two affected flights had landed safely after being affected by bomb threats.
Flights AY1761 from Helsinki to Rome and AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, faced unfounded or hoax bomb threats, the company said.
“Both flights landed safely at their destinations, and customers have disembarked the aircraft,” it said and added that nothing suspicious was found on the planes.
The plane to Rome was inspected and will depart back to Helsinki, while the flight to Vienna will “return to traffic normally after inspection.”
The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, a military escort across at least seven flights in Europe. An airport in Poland was forced to close in a day of chaos on Tuesday.
“Malicious” bomb scares on two flights from London , and others from Manchester, Copenhagen, Israel , Dublin, Bergamo and Lisbon threw airports into disarray, with authorities searching planes after some of the flights were forced to undergo emergency landings.
Hundreds of passengers on board were affected as well as others who had been affected by the temporary closures of airports.
On Wednesday, the French health ministry said that blood banks in France had been hit by a cyberattack amid a series of online hoaxes and cyberattacks.
“Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” the ministry said.
Meanwhile, stores in eight European countries were forced to throw away vast quantities of food after hackers tampered with their fridges on Monday, mirroring hacks that swept dozens of supermarkets in France three weeks ago.

articles.title_orig: Gamers go to ridiculous lengths to “improve” GTA VI with Nvidia’s DLSS 5
articles.title_zh: Gamers go to ridiculous lengths to “improve” GTA VI with Nvidia’s DLSS 5
articles.content_orig:
While the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be available on PC this month, some gamers are making ridiculous preparations to use their PC graphics cards to apply Nvidia’s DLSS 5 technology to the console exclusive.
On an explicitly unmoderated GTAVI subreddit, user RevolutionaryBus8208 lays out a proposed setup, which runs a PlayStation 5 through a 4K capture card to a PC. From there, the video signal is run through Veyra , an open source tool that can apply DLSS 5’s AI-powered “neural rendering” to video content. The result—which also uses DLSS frame generation to increase the 30 fps source to a 90 fps output—is then piped back to a 4K TV, theoretically adding some of the benefits of a beefy PC graphics card to a console-exclusive game.
To demonstrate the potential of this setup, RevolutionaryBus8208 used Veyra to upscale the Grand Theft Auto VI Extended Look trailer posted in August. The resulting DLSS-ified version looks a bit better in places, with sharper background elements, subtler shadows, and more believable light scattering on some surfaces. But it also seems a bit washed out compared to the original video’s deeper blacks and arguably suffers from an unnaturally smooth “soap opera effect” in some scenes.
While the upscaled version causes some occasional graphical artifacts and glitches from the frame generation process, it’s still an interesting proof of concept that shows just how far DLSS 5 has come from some of the early horror-show memes that circulated on the Internet earlier this year.
Of course, running this kind of remote frame generation on a linear video is very different from applying it to a real-time interactive game. While a pure “passthrough” capture card wouldn’t necessarily add any latency itself, any software processing done to get the video feed ready for upscaling—and to do the upscaling itself—could add significant delays between player inputs and on-screen results.
RevolutionaryBus8208 claims that Veyra itself adds a relatively small 11 ms of additional latency to the video source but admits he doesn’t have a capture card to test it with a signal coming from an actual PS5. Other commenters who have tried similar setups with other PS5 games said the input lag was “noticeable but tolerable” or claimed an impossible-to-believe latency addition of “around 1-2 milliseconds.”
For players who can already use Sony’s “PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution” on a PS5 Pro, going through this convoluted process might cause a “hat on a hat” effect. But for stock PS5 owners who happen to have a beefy PC GPU, the hassles and trade-offs might be worth it to get some additional horsepower on console exclusives like GTA VI .
Or, you know, you could just wait for the game’s actual PC release, which is reportedly slated for early 2027 . Or for the likely AI-assisted unofficial decompilation port that should be along any day now.

articles.title_orig: Communist Party of Vietnam delegation pays working visit to China
articles.title_zh: Communist Party of Vietnam delegation pays working visit to China
articles.content_orig:
A delegation of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) led by Nguyen Thanh Nghi, member of the Political Bureau, Secretary of the CPV Central Committee, and head of the committee’s Commission for Policy and Strategy, paid a working visit to China from November 1 to 5. The visit followed the fifth plenary session of the 20th central committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Nghi met with Wang Huning, member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC); held talks with He Lifeng, member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Vice Premier, and Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Financial and Economic Affairs; and had a working session with Lu Hao, member of the CPC Central Committee and Director of the Development Research Centre of the State Council of China.
He congratulated China on its tremendous and comprehensive development achievements and the success of the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, held from October 26–29, describing it as an important theoretical preparation for the CPC’s 21st National Congress. He further expressed confidence that China would successfully implement the Resolution of the 20th National Congress of the CPC, successfully convene the 21st National Congress, and achieve its goal of building China into a modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful.
Nghi also briefed the Chinese side on the implementation of the resolution of Vietnam’s 14th National Party Congress and the country’s socio-economic development, as well as several key policies and orientations adopted at the fourth plenum of the Party Central Committee.
Highlighting the long-standing friendship between Vietnam and China and Vietnam’s policy of giving top priority to developing ties with China, he affirmed that the Vietnamese Party and State stand ready to work with their Chinese counterparts to further strengthen political trust, enhance strategic connectivity, elevate substantive cooperation and support each other in their respective development processes.
Appreciating the significance of the visit, which followed a series of exchanges and meetings between the two countries’ high-ranking leaders, the Chinese leaders affirmed that China always regards relations with Vietnam as a priority in its neighbourhood diplomacy and supports Vietnam in playing a greater international role.
The two sides spoke highly of the positive and comprehensive progress in Vietnam-China relations and agreed to strengthen the leadership and guidance of the two Parties over ministries, sectors, agencies and localities in both countries.
China welcomed Vietnam’s participation in its ‘Big Market for All: Export to China’ initiative. It also expressed readiness to further increase imports of Vietnamese agricultural products and support capable Chinese enterprises in expanding investment in Vietnam.
Following the talks in Beijing the delegation visited Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low, and it adopted a “poison pill” plan that would make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May from Potbelly, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose more than 2% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance during the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's also announced that it has adopted a shareholders' rights plan, a so-called “poison pill,” intended to avert a hostile takeover of the company. The plan, which grants all shareholders except the hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares, automatically triggers if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said. Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy's is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

articles.title_orig: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.title_zh: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.content_orig:
At the invitation of President Xi Jinping, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman paid a state visit to China from November 1 to 2. This was the first China visit by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established 48 years ago in 1978.
Ding Long, a professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University, told Global Times that with tensions mounting in the Strait of Hormuz, and Oman, which has been a long-standing active mediator in regional disputes, coming under pressure as well, the visit reflects the country’s efforts to strengthen strategic support and enhance diplomatic autonomy.
Oman is the only member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to consistently maintain positive relations with Iran, and it has played a pivotal role in regional diplomacy, including hosting rounds of talks between Iran and the United States. Its peaceful policy has earned at least one threat from US President Donald Trump to bomb the country.
Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said on November 2. He said that China stands ready to work with Oman to steer their strategic partnership to a higher level, and to help restore peace and realise lasting stability in the Middle East at an early date. China and Oman, he added, should enhance political mutual trust and strengthen exchanges of experience in national governance, while expressing China’s support for Oman in safeguarding national independence, sovereignty, security and stability, and in independently exploring a development path suited to its national conditions. And China, he said, is ready to deepen the synergy of development strategies with Oman and to be a stable and reliable partner in the energy sector, a partner with promising potential in investment, and a partner in fostering innovation in advanced technologies.
“China has been actively committed to ending hostilities and promoting peace, aiming to contribute its wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security predicament,” Xi said, adding that China will continue to advocate resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, and support regional countries in building a common home of good-neighbourliness, development, security and cooperation.
Stressing that China has been Oman’s largest trading partner for many years and Chinese enterprises’ investment in Oman has kept growing, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said his country is ready to synergise development strategies with China and strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, industry, infrastructure, AI, science and technology, and other fields. He said Oman highly appreciates China’s just position on the Middle East issue and stands ready to maintain close coordination with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote security and stability in the region and beyond.
Later that day, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik met with Chinese Premier Li Qiang. Li said the talks between the two heads of state earlier that morning mapped out a new blueprint for further deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership. He expressed China’s willingness to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Oman, deepen cooperation across the entire oil and gas industry chain, and carry out more high-quality clean energy projects and called on both sides to expand cooperation in areas such as agriculture and fisheries, aerospace satellites, information and communication, and artificial intelligence, and promote the early conclusion of the free trade agreement negotiations between China and the GCC. He stressed that China and Oman, both Global South countries, should maintain close communication and coordination in multilateral affairs to jointly safeguard world peace and stability.
Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said Oman deeply admires China’s development achievements, which have attracted attention worldwide. Oman looks forward to learning from China’s development experience and deepening mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries. Oman is willing to enhance communication and coordination with China in international and regional affairs and to contribute to resolving conflicts and maintaining peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region.
In a potentially significant but under-reported related development, also on November 2, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met separately with the Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and the National Security Advisor of Saudi Arabia.
Meeting with Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Ali Bagheri Kani, Wang Yi stated that China-Iran relations have maintained steady development despite a volatile international landscape. This serves the fundamental interests of both peoples and reflects the aspirations of Global South countries for solidarity and cooperation. China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security and is willing to work with Iran to further advance bilateral relations.
Ali Bagheri Kani briefed Wang Yi on Iran’s views concerning the regional situation, stating that Iran would firmly safeguard its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and resist power politics and threats. Iran is also willing to engage in talks and negotiations with all parties and work actively for regional peace and stability. The Iranian side appreciates the initiatives and proposals put forward by President Xi Jinping and China’s consistent commitment to multilateralism. Iran looks forward to China playing a greater role in international and regional peace. Iran stands ready to promote the steady development of bilateral ties and to strengthen cooperation with China in international and multilateral frameworks.
In his meeting with Wang Yi, Saudi Arabia’s Minister of State, Member of the Council of Ministers, and National Security Advisor Musaad bin Mohammed Al-Aiban handed over a letter from Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman to President Xi Jinping regarding the development of China-Saudi bilateral relations and issues of mutual concern.
Wang Yi said that the current regional situation has once again reached a critical crossroads between war and peace. Although the road to peace is not smooth, it is necessary to keep moving forward. He hoped that all parties would resolve disputes and end the conflict through dialogue and negotiation, safeguarding regional energy and shipping security. China believes that countries in the region should enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust, improve relations, and live harmoniously, promoting the construction of a new regional security framework that serves the long-term interests of their peoples through consultation.
The following articles were originally published by the Xinhua News Agency and on the website of the Chinese Foreign Ministry. The report on Wang Yi’s meeting with the Saudi National Security Advisor was published in Chinese and was machine translated and sub-edited by us.

articles.title_zh: Food delivery startup Wonder files for IPO as it explores its next big bite
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.
Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.
Founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.
Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the company announced it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.
Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The company has outlined ambitious growth plans, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.
Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit company Blue Apron , restaurant delivery platform Grubhub , media company Tastemade , and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.
Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create , its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop new food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.
Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.
Despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

articles.title_orig: Dow plunges 1,200 points, shedding most of midterm results stock rally - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Dow plunges 1,200 points, shedding most of midterm results stock rally - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged about 1,200 points on Thursday, eroding most of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.
The S & P 500 dropped 3.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 4.8%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.
The Dow declined 1,220 points, or 2.2%.
The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.
Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, dropped 7% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fall 12%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 15% in value.
The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.
Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price fall more than 2%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.
The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.
Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.
"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.
Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.
OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.
The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post .

articles.title_orig: So, about that Anthropic IPO . . .
articles.title_zh: So, about that Anthropic IPO . . .
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX’s SPCX recent IPO may have raised some investors’ hopes of using mutual and exchange-traded funds to capture any pop in Anthropic’s pending offering, but they’re unlikely to reap life-changing riches that way.
First, most funds already mark their positions near the expected IPO value, limiting upside potential. Second, most funds’ stakes in the Claude chatbot creator are very small, meaning the portfolios’ other, larger holdings will water down any gains. Finally, as SpaceX showed, early IPO pops can deflate quickly, and timing postoffering sales is not easy.
Funds’ per-share, split-adjusted Anthropic values ranged from Franklin Templeton’s $58.90, as of its Sept. 30, 2026, portfolios, to T. Rowe Price’s $91.65, as of Oct. 30—a massive 55% difference. Timing could explain some of the gap; Franklin’s calculation appears to reflect Anthropic’s last May 2026 financing round price, without subsequent adjustments. It’s possible the firm has revised its numbers since the frontier artificial intelligence lab filed its S-1 IPO prospectus in October.
Still, timing does not account for all differences. Looking only at Sept. 30 portfolios, per-share values ranged from ClearBridge Select Fund’s LBFIX $58.90 (ClearBridge is a subsidiary of Franklin Templeton), seemingly reflecting Anthropic’s last financing round, to Tema Electrification ETF’s VOLT $85.10—a still-massive 44% difference. Given that Anthropic’s last financing round in May 2026 valued the company at $965 billion, that implies a $400 billion to $500 billion gap between ClearBridge’s estimated Anthropic value versus Tema’s and T. Rowe’s marks, a gap roughly equivalent to the size of the 20th largest company in the S&P 500.
Assuming those values have not converged, ClearBridge’s discounted Anthropic valuation relative to Tema or T. Rowe seems to offer an opportunity to realize more appreciation if the AI company’s shares jump after its IPO. Given recent reporting that Anthropic is targeting a $1.5 trillion valuation, outside of the ClearBridge fund, much of the upside is already baked into mutual funds and ETFs’ net asset values, so there are no massive gains to be had for investors based purely on the expected IPO price.
Why do these valuations vary so much? Mutual funds and ETFs have significant leeway in valuing private companies, since such holdings rarely have observable trading prices. In practice, many asset managers anchor to the most recent financing round (Anthropic last raised money in May at a $965 billion valuation, or about $589 per share) and adjust based on market conditions or big secondary market trades. That still leaves a lot of room for disagreement among fund firms, especially when AI-related stocks post wide daily swings, as they have recently. As a result, valuation is often in the eye of the beholder.
Reported valuations can be stale, too. Mutual funds often disclose their portfolios 30 days after month- or quarter-end, so the Anthropic valuations we see could be different from what funds think it is worth in real time. Anthropic also disclosed in its S-1 that it did a 10-for-1 share split in September, so reported per-share valuations can also look 10 times higher than they truly are.
In addition to the potential return difference that different valuations can cause, investors seeking pre-IPO exposure to Anthropic should note most funds and ETFs do not have large Anthropic positions. Only one has more than 5% of its portfolio in the company, and even at that level, the AI lab could double its value and the fund would see just a 5% gain, before factoring in how the other 95% of the portfolio performs.
Of course, there is also no guarantee that Anthropic’s stock will rise post-IPO, and potential share price volatility can make timing an exit even harder, as SpaceX has shown. Despite SpaceX’s massive rally in its first few days of trading (it nearly doubled by its third day of trading), it now trades near its IPO offer price.
Thus, given funds’ and ETFs’ small helpings of Anthropic, the baked-in valuations, and the uncertainty over the direction, magnitude, and duration of its shares’ post-IPO performance, it’s not worth it for most investors to buy a mutual fund or ETF simply to get short-term exposure to Anthropic’s historic IPO.

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman unseats Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, another win for the left in a major city
Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of an artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped as much as 6.2%, before rebounding to trade lower by about 4.5% throughout the late morning.
The S&P 500 also rebounded from earlier losses, but was still down 3.1%, putting it on track for its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” territory on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting  bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
The two companies were among the worst performers on the Nasdaq indexes, sliding 12%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
Memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron were among the S&P 500’s biggest losers, all plunging around around 15%.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. As of midmorning trading, Brent and U.S. crude oil rose 2%.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,250 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.title_zh: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.
Thursday did a lot of the damage. At its morning low, Nvidia was down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a matter of hours and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. A close there would be the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.
Nvidia has plenty of company.
AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) are posting steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) are falling near 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is now more than a third below its June record.
Nvidia itself is down nearly 25% from its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .
The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.
Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.
The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.
That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.
For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.
"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

articles.title_orig: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.title_zh: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.content_orig:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years as it warned that inflation is surging towards 5pc.
Policymakers voted to raise rates to 4pc from 3.75pc on Thursday in the first increase since August 2023.
The Bank blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East for triggering another sharp jump in energy prices, with John Healey’s maiden Budget doing little to ease a two-year decline in household incomes.
Threadneedle Street now believes inflation will peak around 5pc by the middle of 2027, even if the economy slows sharply.
However, policymakers said price rises would hit 6pc next summer if the Iran war drags on.
The Bank also laid bare the impact of the conflict on family finances, with Donald Trump’s war pushing up mortgage costs for the average household by £1,500.
The Ofgem energy price cap is now expected to rise by more than £400 to £2,150 in January, with the Chancellor’s £100 Budget handout doing little to mitigate the increase.
Andrew Bailey said growing price pressures from the prolonged war in Iran meant Thursday’s increase was unlikely to be the last.
Other members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the prospect of another rate rise before Christmas.
One member, Catherine Mann, called for an immediate 0.5 percentage point jump to 4.25pc.
Thanks for following our coverage of the Bank of England’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.
Andrew Bailey said there was a “strong” case for more rate rises as the Iran war ramps up inflation pressures on the economy.
You can keep up to date with the latest here .
Analysts at Goldman Sachs were surprised by the signals from the Bank of England that more interest rates were likely.
Andrew Bailey said he could “see the argument of a further increase in rates”, with fellow policymakers Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill and Megan Greene also indicating further increases were on the cards.
The views of other rate setters also surprised Goldman.
James Moberly, an economist at the Wall Street bank, said: “We had not expected Catherine Mann to support a larger hike, and had anticipated that Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra would prefer to hold.”
The FTSE 100 in London remains up 0.7pc despite the Bank of England signalling more interest rate rises could be on the way.
However, US tech stocks continued their falls this week in the wake of the midterm elections.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 1.2pc to 25,427.44 at the open on Wall Street, while the benchmark S&P 500 fell 0.4pc to 7,654.89.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5pc to 53,595.12 as investors switched out of tech stocks into more traditional sectors, over fears the Democrats would limit expansion of AI companies.
Traders expect too many interest rate rises from the Bank of England over the next year, an investment manager has warned.
April LaRusse, co-head of client portfolio management at BNY Investments, said money markets were anticipating too many further rate rises.
Traders are betting that the Bank will raise rates to 4.75pc by the end of next summer.
She said: “While we believe today’s increase was important in reinforcing the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, markets may now be somewhat too aggressive in the scale of further tightening they are pricing.
“Growth continues to benefit from strong business investment, particularly around AI-related infrastructure, but beyond this area we expect the economy to soften through 2027.
“Against that backdrop, the hurdle for further rate increases is likely to rise after the initial few hikes.”
Telegraph readers said inflation feels much more severe than the Bank of England’s forecasts of around 5pc in the early months of next year.
Here are some views from the comments section below and you can join the debate here .
Households face a “clear risk” that the Bank of England will raise interest rates in December after putting up borrowing costs for the first time in three years on Thursday.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said the “balance of risks has shifted” in favour of higher inflation, after policymakers forecast prices could rise at an annual pace of around 5pc early next year.
He said the latest rate rise was an “insurance policy” against the risk of inflation rising further and said he did not expect several increases in the future.
But he warned: “The bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February.
“There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).”
Andrew Bailey, coming towards the end of his press conference, said he hopes there will be more information on whether the Iran war will end by the Bank of England’s next meeting in December.
Answering a question from Telegraph economics editor Szu Ping Chan , he said: “We will judge this at each meeting.
“We will inevitably have more information by December because we will get more data releases and so on.
“I hope we will also have more information on where this conflict is going to. That would be the most important thing.”
Andrew Bailey said he “could see the case” for a further quarter point increase in interest rates to 4.25pc if the Middle East war is not resolved.
The Governor also said he would not sign up to suggestions that households faced just two rate rises as a result of the war.
“I’m not going to sign up to the two-and-done point,” he said.
Any further increase in interest rates would come down to “risk judgement”.
He said: “Things have happened in the last 48 hours but the whole situation is so volatile that we really don’t want to put much weight on two days, which frankly haven’t yet been backed by any firm evidence that there is a peace process which is going to lead to something concrete.”
Traders are betting it is a coin toss whether the Bank of England will raise interest rates for a second time before Christmas.
Money markets suggest there is a 53pc chance policymakers will vote for the Bank Rate to be lifted for a second meeting in a row to 4.25pc in December.
Traders had given a second rate rise this year a 30pc chance before the Bank announced it was raising rates from 3.75pc to 4pc.
However, they increased bets on higher rates after Andrew Bailey, the Governor, said there was a “strong” case for a second rate rise if the Iran war was not brought to an end.
John Healey has been urged to cut benefits and lower taxes after inflation rose to 4pc.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Rising interest rates are another headwind for hardworking families to deal with.
“They mean higher mortgage costs, and with the independent OBR confirming that living standards will fall next year, it’s time Labour cut taxes, welfare spending and costly regulations to make life cheaper for families.”
“The tax burden is expected to hit a record high in the wake of Mr Healey’s first Budget last week.”
Andrew Bailey called for an end to the Iran war to end the inflation pressure facing households this winter.
The Governor of the Bank of England said he was unable to tell people how high interest rates would go but said the best way to resolve price pressures in the economy was for the Middle East conflict to come to an end.
He said: “Inflation is bad for everybody... it is most difficult for those on low incomes and those struggling to find work.
“We are very conscious of the need to deal with this.
“In conditions that are as uncertain as the ones we face, I cannot give any assurances to people about where are interest rates going to go to.
“All I would come back to... and this was the same message as the Prime Minister gave yesterday, actually, which I firmly agree with, the focus must now be on dealing with this conflict, ending this conflict.
