articles.title_orig: Wall Street Is Already Bracing for a 2027 Debt Ceiling Fight - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Is Already Bracing for a 2027 Debt Ceiling Fight - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Democrats just won big, and bond investors are already eyeing the next showdown. Treasury's borrowing room is shrinking faster than its plans suggest, and one corner of the market may carry far more risk than Wednesday's rally implies.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Stocks and long-term Treasurys both rose on November 4, 2026, after Democrats swept the midterms. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) gained 1.65% to $766.82. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF ( NASDAQ:TLT ) rose 0.8% to $81.76.
Analyst notes still turned to the next fight: a 2027 debt ceiling that Democrats can now use as leverage, and TLT owns the part of the Treasury market most exposed to a long standoff.
The 2025 reconciliation law raised the limit by $5 trillion, from $36.1 trillion to $41.1 trillion. This year’s deficit came to $1.99 trillion.
One Wednesday count had Democrats on track for at least 54 Senate seats and 250 House seats, with two Senate races still uncalled.
Democrats have not announced any demands. Before the vote, on October 27, Trump said he would find a way to work with them and pointed to his veto power.
Treasury data show $40.547 trillion in total public debt on November 3, against a statutory limit of $41.104 trillion. Once you remove debt not subject to the limit, that leaves about $754 billion of room.
Treasury expects $800 billion in privately held net borrowing from January through March. That figure measures something different from debt subject to the limit, but it suggests the remaining room is smaller than next quarter’s planned borrowing.
Treasury has not given an X-date, meaning the day it could no longer pay all its bills on time. The Bipartisan Policy Center offers a preliminary estimate. Its June 4 projection puts the limit most likely to be reached between late winter and mid-summer of 2027, with extraordinary measures lasting six to nine months after that. Wall Street estimates put the X-date in the fourth quarter of 2027.
Robert Sockin, chief US economist at PGIM, said a technical default is not the firm’s base case, although the risk is higher than ever. If one did happen, he warned of more US downgrades, higher long-term yields and a very negative reaction in stocks, which is where SPY is exposed.
Long bonds take that hit first. When the term premium (the extra yield investors demand for lending over long periods) goes up, a thirty-year bond loses far more value than a two-year note.
On Wednesday, the ten-year yield fell to 4.90% from 4.95%, the thirty-year fell to 5.28% from 5.32%, and the two-year fell to 4.58% from 4.61%. Even so, TLT trades much closer to its 52-week low of $76.43 than to its high of $90.86.
Next week’s refunding will test demand.
Treasury’s $125 billion refunding includes $58 billion of three-year notes, $42 billion of ten-year notes and $25 billion of thirty-year bonds, raising about $28 billion in new cash. It also dropped “at least” from its guidance on keeping auction sizes steady, and analysts read that as leaving room for changes in the first half of 2027, although the releases do not mention the debt limit.
My view is that TLT carries more risk than Wednesday’s rally suggests. Wednesday’s rally brought some rate relief. But TLT holds the longest Treasurys, and that is where a 2027 standoff, downgrades, and steady supply would hurt the most.
Short-term Treasury notes carry less of that exposure, because the two-year pays 4.58% with much less price risk. Bills that mature near a late-2027 X-date carry their own standoff risk, so maturities outside that window avoid that specific risk.
The October jobs report comes out on Friday, November 6, at 8:30 a.m. ET, and after that you can check demand at next week’s auctions. A formal Democratic demand would raise the risk. So would an updated X-date estimate, and a TLT close below $76.43 would show long-term bond prices are reflecting that risk.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.content_orig:
At least five tankers have been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian forces said, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the United States and Israel’s war on the country is unresolved.
Since the war on Iran began in late February, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
“Last night … a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt,” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) told the Fars news agency on Thursday.
“Another supertanker was halted by a massive fire while exiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz. A tugboat that had approached the supertanker to extinguish the fire also caught fire,” the IRGC added.
The Iranian army later said three more tankers were hit by naval mines and caught fire.
“Early this morning, a violating oil tanker – navigating through an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz – caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine,” the army said, according to the official IRNA news agency.
“Today at around noon, two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz,” said another army statement carried by IRNA.
Separately, the British military said a tanker was struck by two projectiles off Qatar’s coast.
The vessel was hit about 50 nautical miles (about 93 kilometres) north of Qatar’s ⁠Madinat ash-Shamal on Wednesday at 23:20 GMT, the ⁠United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Thursday.
UKMTO did not identify the tanker or which country’s flag it was sailing under. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack.
In an incident last week, a Qatari tanker was hit by “unidentified objects” while sailing in the Gulf.
The liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda was hit on October 30, the Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat) said on Sunday.
No crew members were injured, and there ‌was no environmental impact, the company said, adding that the vessel remained ‌safe and ‌operational while the impact was being assessed.
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are still running close to a record pace.
UKMTO said in a report last month that it was “struggling to accurately report” the true number of attacks as the majority of ships now refuse to report them.
Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts to resume talks on ending the war in recent days.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson said on Tuesday that ⁠both sides were reviewing proposals ⁠put forward by mediators, with talks continuing.
But unnamed Pentagon officials and military commanders told The New York Times on Wednesday that thousands of US air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the US are poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on President Donald Trump’s orders.
Iranian government and military leaders, however, have warned of repercussions if the US or Israel pursue further military action.
On Wednesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power.
IRGC Ground Force commander Brigadier General Mohammad Karami said on Wednesday that the continuation of “hostile and brutal actions by Iran’s enemies” would lead to “further Iranian victories and greater national pride”, while accelerating the expulsion of foreign powers from the region and the collapse of Israel.

articles.title_orig: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.title_zh: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.content_orig:
The Joint List alliance of Arab-led parties says it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government after last week’s election.
“The Joint List announced today, Thursday, that it will inform the President of the State, Isaac Herzog, this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government,” the alliance said in a statement.
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election, a result that could give them significant influence over the formation of the next government.
Once the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers formally submit their recommendation, Eisenkot is expected to have the backing of 67 lawmakers, exceeding the 61-seat majority threshold in the Knesset.
Earlier, Ra’am, an Arab-led party with eight seats, said it would also recommend Eisenkot.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats may not yield 53 endorsements, as Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate.
The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Netanyahu has also claimed repeatedly and without evidence that Arab parties committed fraud during the elections with foreign backing.
The prime minister and his Likud party have cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists who allegedly bribed voters before polls opened. They are suspected of connections with the Ra’am party, although the party denies any involvement.
Netanyahu and Likud also suggested that the opposition bloc joining with Arab-led parties would be treasonous. In a statement after the vote, Likud warned that Zionist parties cooperating with the Arab bloc would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the results of the election on Wednesday after finding no evidence of fraud.
President Herzog has also accepted the results and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
He also backed investigating suspected interference but warned against smearing voters who are Palestinian citizens of Israel, saying he had “great respect” for the country’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.
On Wednesday, the president said he had met representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas and Yisrael Beytenu factions.
In a post on X, Herzog said he “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned”.
Herzog added that talks would also continue on Thursday.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said that if Eisenkot is able to form a government, then he will become Israel’s next prime minister and Netanyahu will likely be the head of the opposition.
“It is up to Gadi Eisenkot to do what he promised, to oust Benjamin Netanyahu. And to do that, he needs to have 61 votes in the Knesset, which means that he needs the votes of the Palestinian-Israeli parties, parties that he does not want to partner up with,” she said.
“But he will most likely have to reach some sort of deal, for [the Palestinian-Israeli parties] to abstain at the very least, to make sure that his government is sworn in and a new chapter in Israeli politics is able to begin,” she added.

articles.title_orig: Micron stock declines 12% as chip sell-off deepens
articles.title_zh: Micron stock declines 12% as chip sell-off deepens
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”
Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.
The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.
Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police have fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles have broken out in Nantes and authorities have arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by almost 600,000 people – have remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike is organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors have been impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.
In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.
The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near standstill at points by the sheer quantity of people.
Later, several protesters were seen lying on the ground being treated by street medics, with blood flowing from the head of an older man. A bystander said the man was struck by police, but an officer at the scene said they were unaware of any incident.
At one point, protesters scattered as tear gas was deployed by police, followed by mass cries of “everyone hates the police.”
The mood of the crowd has lost its upbeat feel.
Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers, have called for a nationwide strike. So, how is that affecting these essential services?
Schools: About 13% of all school staff are participating in the strikes, France’s education ministry estimates, including 16% of all teachers. Around 19% of schools and 18% of colleges across France are affected by the strike.
Universities: About one in three of France’s higher education are “disrupted” because of the strikes and protests, the government told CNN.
Hospitals: Very few public hospital staff – only about 4% of the workforce – are participating in the strike, France’s healthcare ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Two of France’s main unions representing both public and private healthcare workers had called on them to strike, citing the high cost of living and the deterioriation of public services.
Transport: Four in 10 of today’s scheduled trains have been canceled, though a handful of those cancelations are due to other factors like unavailable equipment, according to tracking website Trayn.
The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the largest of the unions – the CGT – says the minimum wage needs to be increased immediately by 10%.
Last month, the CGT claimed there had been a big increase in the number of professions paying some employees less than the minimum wage. Another union - the CFDT – is demanding a 100 euro increase in the minimum monthly wage, about 7%.
Maud Millier, a CGT official in Lyon, said that the government’s announced minimum wage increase, from November 1, amounts to just €15 for someone earning the minimum wage, which she said was nowhere near enough given rising fuel and food pr

articles.title_orig: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.title_zh: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG , Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and Global Cybersecurity Alliance Limited (GCSA) have announced the joint establishment of the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research. The initiative brings together both parties' technological expertise and industry resources in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and industrial applications to advance research, product innovation, and industry collaboration.
Founded in 1982, China Resources Longdation operates across property management, asset management, and community services. Its Aethereal Cybersecurity business specializes in AI-driven digital transformation and cybersecurity services for government agencies and enterprises, providing professional technologies and solutions to Hong Kong SAR 's government departments, public institutions, and businesses, supported by relevant cybersecurity qualifications. GCSA is committed to advancing technological innovation, research collaboration, and international exchange in cybersecurity, with a particular focus on emerging security challenges involving AI, Web3, and digital finance.
The two parties will strengthen their cooperation in cybersecurity. The Centre will focus on joint research and development in AI-powered fraud prevention, cyber threat detection, digital financial security, and cybersecurity automation. Key areas of exploration include AI deception honeypots, intelligent fraud detection, threat intelligence analysis, and security platforms, with an emphasis on practical applications.
By combining their respective resources and professional service capabilities, the partnership aims to foster cross-organizational collaboration in AI and cybersecurity, contributing to the development of the digital economy and cybersecurity industry.
Contact: Laber Mann, media@gcsa.com

articles.title_orig: Shield AI To Hit $28.8 Billion Value With $5.3 Billion Radar Acquisition
articles.title_zh: Shield AI To Hit $28.8 Billion Value With $5.3 Billion Radar Acquisition
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Defense tech firm Shield AI is acquiring Echodyne , a provider of counter-drone radar systems, in a $5.3 billion deal, the companies announced today.
The deal, which is expected to close in early 2027, will give Shield an in-house counter-UAS offering, according to a company statement. Echodyne says its counter-drone systems are “used by defense, government and commercial customers in more than 40 countries.” Further, its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) system was selected in September by the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to supply counter-drone systems to the US military.
The addition of a counter-drone radar system is an interesting add to Shield, which has several different product lines, ranging from autonomy software that has been used on multiple Pentagon projects, to the large X-Bat drone the company now hopes to market globally .
Shield has a history of product expansion through acquisition. It’s V-Bat drone, and hence the push for X-Bat, came form a 2021 acquisition of Martin UAV. And earlier this year, the firm closed on the purchase of Aechelon Technologies, a simulation software firm.
“The acquisition of Echodyne dramatically accelerates our efforts to meet growing customer demand for multi-mission capabilities, provides increased access to a rapidly expanding counter-drone industry, and further diversifies our revenue streams with sustained, compelling growth for the combined company,” Shield CEO Gary Steele said in a statement, noting the company structure now consists of three buckets: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems.
“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations. Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg added. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”
Echodyne will operate as a business unit within Shield’s mission systems business, with Frankenberg staying on and reporting up to Steele as part of the company’s executive team. There are no planned workforce reductions, and Echodyne employees will not be required to relocate, according to a Shield spokesperson. Longer term, there will likely be greater integration of Echodyne products across Shield’s portfolio.
A commitment to long-term operational value.
While the company is not announcing any “specific aircraft integrations” right now, the spokesperson noted that “Autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and Shield expects autonomous aircraft to need more capable onboard sensors in the coming years. Echodyne’s radar is built for that use. The acquisition also adds radar engineering, manufacturing capacity and a commercial customer base to Shield’s business.”
The spokesperson added that the Echodyne deal has no impact on the recent decision to work with RTX for a radar on X-Bat, saying that work “is separate from this acquisition.”
Of the $5.3 billion deal, $4.8 billion will be paid out at closing with another $500 million paid out upon Echodyne meeting spelled out performance targets. Coinciding with the deal, Shield raised $2.5 billion through Series H funding and investments from Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase.
The spokesperson also noted that the company “will continue to look at acquisitions as part of its growth strategy.”

articles.title_zh: Sony revives its classic 1979 Walkman headphones for modern listeners – with a surprisingly affordable price - What Hi-Fi?
articles.content_orig:
The latest hi-fi, home cinema and tech news, reviews, buying advice and deals, direct to your inbox.
Your newsletter sign-up was successful
When Sony launched the first Walkman (TPS-L2) in 1979 , the wired headphones it made to go along with this new portable tape player were the slim and lightweight Sony MDR-3.
And now, nearly five decades later, Sony is bringing them back. Enter the all-new, but very familiar-looking Sony MDR-3R wired headphones with a USB-C connection.
Capitalising on the popular trend for wired headphones and all things retro, particularly among the younger generation, these on-ears aim to "bring the spirit of that iconic model" along with a few modern updates.
The new MDR-3R are practically identical in design to the original headphones from 1979. Sony says that although the MDR-3 was developed over 40 years ago, it was already a pretty "complete product design".
The new cans have the same slender adjustable metal headband, with the characteristic angular fold before it meets the earcup housings, and are super lightweight at just 38g.
Two sets of colourful foam earpads – blue and orange – are included in the box. Sony has even taken pains to make sure the retail box and instruction manual of the new headphones are identical to the original packaging as well.
The MDR-3R has been "re-engineered with the same 23mm driver units" based on the original drawings of the MDR-3. The aim is to stay "true to the original sound signature", while offering a wider frequency range and better bass quality.
The latest hi-fi, home cinema and tech news, reviews, buying advice and deals, direct to your inbox.
Sony says the new cans should deliver "rich, clear vocals" that work well with "modern music".
The earcups also feature "sound holes", as Sony calls them, meaning the new MDR-3R are an open acoustic design just like their originals. That should be good news for sound quality, but less so for those around you, as open designs tend to leak sound.
It's an interesting choice for a modern portable pair. Sony tells us there is "some sound leakage", but not too much. We'll be curious to find out how it performs in real-life use, and if there's enough leakage to be a nuisance on the train or in the office.
How else has Sony modernised this retro design? Instead of a 3.5mm connection, you get a USB-C cable for connecting to more recent smartphones and laptops.
This cable also features a built-in microphone and in-line controls, with a three-button system that lets you control playback, skip tracks, change volume, take hands-free calls, and even summon your phone's voice assistant.
There's no official IP rating, and as these are wired, there's no Bluetooth, battery life or noise-cancelling to worry about.
The new Sony MDR-3R wired headphones are available from November at a surprisingly budget price of £49 / $60 / €59.
A limited edition Stranger Things model – with a black headband with an engraved Stranger Things logo, and black and red earpads – will also be released for £59 / $80 / €69.
Will Sony be able to replicate its incredible wireless headphones success with this new wired model? We can't wait to find out. Now, if only it could also release an affordable Walkman music player alongside it…

articles.title_orig: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.title_zh: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike.
Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas.
Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police.
Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).
“Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added.
In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans.
Around 250 rallies against rising living costs had been planned in cities and towns across the country and hundreds of thousands of people would likely turn out, unions said before the events kicked off.
France’s main unions, including the CGT and CNT representing public and private sector workers, and the UNEF, representing students, warned the government of President Emmanuel Macron’s that the country was on the brink or recession.
“Everything is going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement. “Anger is immense.”
“The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay,” the statement added.
The movement grew from a student protest over staff shortages at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris. Videos of the blockade spread on social media, and soon protests expanded to high schools across the nation.
As the movement grew, the list of grievances expanded beyond the failings of the public school system to encompass broader economic, political and social dissatisfaction. Soon, university students, teachers, parents and politicians also joined.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters have since taken to the streets as the demonstrations expanded, with participants holding signs criticizing the far-right National Rally party and warning of the risks of climate change and artificial intelligence. A multitude of Palestinian flags have also been seen.
Macron, who will leave office in May, convened a defense ‌and security meeting Wednesday ahead of the protests. Later, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers would be deployed Thursday, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters.
Police have previously been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics. Last month, a 15-year-old was maimed by a sting ball grenade fired by police and a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture in a similar incident.
Several other have also suffered life-changing injuries and a 59-year-old man, identified as Christophe M, died Oct. 17 of “a critical cardio-respiratory failing” after leaving Paris’ Place de la République which had been tear-gassed be police. An investigation into his death is ongoing.
Zacharie Petit reported from Paris and Henry Austin from London.
Zacharie Petit is a producer in Paris.
Henry Austin is a senior editor for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.title_zh: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.content_orig:
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".
Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".
The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.
In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".
It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".
The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.
On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.
Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".
The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.
Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.
However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that  process, the tribunal heard.
He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.
The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".
The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.
On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".
Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".
The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on its menu.

articles.title_orig: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.title_zh: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Great Wealth Transfer is starting to impact the housing market.
A record share of first-time homebuyers are paying for their properties in cash, a sign that more buyers are likely using money they inherited from older generations to help fund their purchases.
Last year, 1 in 10 first-time buyers did an all-cash transaction, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors, the fourth straight year with an increase, and the largest share since the trade group began collecting data on those transactions in 2003. Among first-time all-cash buyers, 28% reported using an inheritance to help fund their deal, compared with just 9% of first-time buyers who financed.
As home prices hover near all-time highs and mortgage rates stay north of 7% , pricing out many prospective buyers, some portion of those buyers may simply be waiting for an inheritance or other significant help from wealthy baby boomers or members of the Silent Generation.
"It is critical when analyzing first-time buyers to understand there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth," the report said.
Buyers reliant on wealth transfers look different from those who finance and use their own savings. As modern life expectancy increases, delaying inheritances, first-time all-cash buyers are typically deep into middle age. The median first-time buyer paying all cash is 54 years old, according to the report, significantly older than the median age of 38 for first-time buyers financing their homes.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

German police have launched an investigation after a senior politician was found dead in a hotel room in Berlin on Wednesday evening.
Authorities are probing whether a third party was involved in the death of Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier of the state of Bavaria and leader of a small conservative party.
Mr Aiwanger, 55, who served as the economy minister in Germany’s largest state, was due to give a speech at the opening of an office for his Free Voters party, but missed the occasion because he felt unwell, German outlet Bild reported.
“The aim of the inquest is to establish the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, and to rule out any possible third-party culpability,” Berlin police and prosecutors said in a statement, giving no further details.
“The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is a terrible tragedy. We are all deeply shocked,” Bavarian premier Markus Soeder said in a statement published on the state government website.
“Our thoughts are first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them.”
A statement on the regional government’s website said it “mourns” the loss of the 55-year-old.
Bild reported that he was found in the Hotel Neuer Fritz in central Berlin. Police cars and several state government cars were parked outside the hotel that evening.
After he reported being unwell, staff members believed he might be suffering an infection, while members of the CSU parliamentary group said he had been experiencing gastrointestinal problems, the outlet reported.
The Berlin public prosecutor’s office told Bild that there is “no initial suspicion of a crime” but that “nothing can be ruled out”. The outlet reported that Mr Aiwanger’s body had no external injuries.
The Free Voters of Bavaria have been in a coalition with the conservative Christian Social Union in the state since 2018.
He joined the party in 2002 and first became a member of the county council in Landshut in 2004.
Mr Aiwanger was elected federal chair of the party in 2010, before the party sent its first MEP, Ulrike Mueller, to the European parliament in 2014.
He had two children with long-term partner Tanja Schweiger.

A Canadian woman and her daughter were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack over the weekend while hiking on a trail near their home, according to authorities.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, an art therapist, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, went missing Saturday after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail, just minutes from their home in Bella Coola, British Columbia .
Loved ones grew concerned when Balcarras failed to show up for a scheduled online meet-up on Saturday, her brother, Matt Balcarras, told The Vancouver Sun .
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack. (Facebook/Josh Kara Balcarras)
A PRACTICAL GUIDE TO NOT GETTING MAULED BY A BEAR WHILE HIKING OR CAMPING THIS SUMMER
After failing to reach the pair, relatives asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) for a welfare check on Sunday morning.
Authorities discovered Balcarras' vehicle parked at the trailhead . Her body was recovered Monday, and search teams found Reed's body on Tuesday.
A Grizzly bear in Jasper National Park, Canada. A Canadian woman and her daughter were killed in a suspected bear attack in British Columbia over the weekend, conservation officials said. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL
"There was evidence to suggest a bear may have been involved," Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service, said in a video update posted to social media.
Tyre noted that officers were actively working to "locate and capture any bears involved" and said it was not immediately clear if more than one animal was responsible.

"Any captured bear will be assessed," conservation officials added in a statement. "If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety."
Matt Balcarras expressed shock over the location of the attack, emphasizing that his sister and niece were experienced in the region.
"They were not naive city folks," he said. "They were strong women living the life."

articles.title_orig: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.title_zh: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title_orig: YouTube rolling out app redesign without Subscriptions tab, and everyone hates it
articles.title_zh: YouTube rolling out app redesign without Subscriptions tab, and everyone hates it
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Google seems to be taking multiple stabs at tweaking how the bottom navigation bar in the YouTube app looks and works. After removing the Subscriptions tab from the navigation bar , the company is now experimenting with a new floating design.
According to a Reddit post by user SameRecognition5543, Google has started testing a floating navigation bar in the YouTube app on Android. The design looks heavily inspired by the Liquid Glass aesthetic of iOS 27, leading some users to accuse Google of abandoning its own Material 3 Expressive design language in favor of Apple’s Liquid Glass.
Google seems to be running a very limited test for the floating navigation bar on Android. We checked on multiple devices and couldn’t spot the new navigation bar test on any of them. However, we did spot the new floating navigation bar on a couple of iPhones. Google may be prioritizing an iPhone rollout first, which makes sense since iOS introduced the Liquid Glass design language.
Meanwhile, if you like the new look and don’t want to wait for Google to eventually roll it out to your device, there is a workaround you can use. The Morphe YouTube patcher has already been updated with a similar floating navigation bar featuring a Liquid Glass design. First, enable pre-release patches in Morphe on your Android phone. Then, go to Settings > General > Navigation bar and turn on the “Enable glass navigation bar” toggle.
User opinion on the new floating navigation bar is split. Several users are waiting for the update to reach their devices and are using Morphe in the meantime. However, other users aren’t too happy about the iOS-like design. Either way, this might well be the future of YouTube’s navigation bar on Android. If you don’t like it, you can take solace in the fact that Google’s rollouts are infamously slow and phased, so you might not have to see it for a while, even when it does start rolling out.

articles.title_orig: Why Sandisk Stock Keeps Going Down
articles.title_zh: Why Sandisk Stock Keeps Going Down
articles.content_orig:
For investors, it's not as much fun owning Sandisk ( SNDK -19.20% ) as it once was.
Shares of Sandisk, one of the world's leading producers of NAND flash memory for PCs, mobile devices, and -- increasingly -- artificial intelligence data centers , are still up 400% over the past 52 weeks. That's great for investors who got in on the ground floor. More recent Sandisk investors, however, have suffered terribly as Sandisk shares shed 36% of their value over just the last six trading days.
And as of 10 a.m. ET Thursday, Sandisk stock is down another 14.5%.
Image source: Getty Images.
Why is Sandisk stock still going down? Some blame Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT, which has been in the news a lot lately for boasting it invented a new "4F square" memory chip and plans to market it as high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers.
Earlier today, CXMT announced it's received $1 billion in customer prepayments for its DRAM chips through the end of September, "a 15.7-fold increase from ... the end of 2025," according to DigiTimes.
NASDAQ · As of 1:58 PM ET 11/05/26
Should this worry Sandisk investors? Not necessarily.
Firstly, investors need to remember that although both CXMT and Sandisk make computer memory , CXMT focuses on DRAM, while Sandisk produces NAND flash memory exclusively. While competing tangentially in the "memory market," CXMT is not a direct competitor to Sandisk.
One area where the companies may compete in future is if Sandisk's invention of high-bandwidth flash (HBF) memory takes off as an alternative to HBM and CXMT succeeds in producing DRAM chips capable of being used as HBM. As DigiTimes reports, however, CXMT is struggling to transition its DRAM to HBM, and yield rates for its "next-generation HBM3E products" are only 20% to 30%.
If that's the best CXMT can do, Sandisk investors may have even less to worry about .

SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) stocks extended declines on Thursday, each dropping roughly 9%. Shares of the Elon Musk-led companies were pounded after Democrats won control of the House and Senate this week, raising concerns over regulatory hurdles for data center buildouts in the US and merger aspirations between the two companies.
The Democratic win in Texas, where both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered, is at the center of the concern. The state flipped blue at the gubernatorial level and saw the Senate seat won by James Talarico, with whom Musk got into fierce spats on social media leading up to the elections.
"We will believe a SpaceX/Tesla merger happens but now faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap to get this deal done in 2027 given this new political blue roadmap in DC/Texas," Yorkville's partner and managing director Dan Ives wrote on Thursday.
Elon Musk said on SpaceX's third quarter earnings call last month that he thinks merging the company with Tesla ( TSLA ) would be a good idea and revealed that both companies are exploring a potential deal.
Earlier this year, Musk also announced the launch of a Terafab, a massive semiconductor manufacturing complex in Texas that would supply SpaceX and Tesla.
Worries over a slowdown in data center build-outs also dampened shares of Texas-based SpaceX, which has increasingly leaned into AI compute as a revenue source.
Ives said while Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027, the growth rate into 2028 "will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map, especially in the state of Texas."
On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs analysts also calculated, "Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.

articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

articles.title_orig: AppLovin stock soars after Q3 earnings, outlook beat
articles.title_zh: AppLovin stock soars after Q3 earnings, outlook beat
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Mobile app technology company AppLovin ( APP ) (NASDAQ:APP) announced better-than-expected revenue in Q3 2026, with revenue up 55.5% year on year to $2.18 billion. In addition, next quarter's revenue guidance ($2.38 billion at the midpoint) was surprisingly strong and 5.5% above analysts' consensus estimates. Its GAAP profit of $4.30 per share was 6.6% above analysts' consensus estimates.
For more on AppLovin, read our full research report .
AppLovin stock rose 18% before the bell on Thursday.
Revenue $2.18 billion vs analysts' consensus estimates of $2.07 billion, according to S&P (55.5% year-on-year growth, 5.4% beat)
EPS (GAAP) $4.30 vs analysts' consensus estimates of $4.03 (6.6% beat)
Adjusted EBITDA $1.84 billion vs analysts' consensus estimates of $1.73 billion (84.3% margin, 6.3% beat)
Revenue guidance $2.38 billion at the midpoint for Q4 2026, above analysts' consensus estimates of $2.25 billion
EBITDA guidance $2.01 billion at the midpoint for Q4 2026, above analysts' consensus estimates of $1.88 billion
Operating margin 78.2%, up from 76.8% in the same quarter last year
Free cash flow margin 64.9%, up from 45.2% in the previous quarter
Market capitalization $82.16 billion
A company's long-term revenue performance is one signal of its overall quality. Any business can have short-term success, but a top-tier one grows for years. AppLovin's revenue grew at a solid 24.8% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years. Its growth surpassed the average software company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.
Long-term growth is the most important, but within software, a half-decade historical view may miss new innovations or demand cycles. AppLovin's annualized revenue growth of 39.2% over the last two years is above its five-year trend, suggesting its demand was strong and recently accelerated.
This quarter, AppLovin reported strong year-on-year revenue growth of 55.5%, and its $2.18 billion of revenue beat Wall Street's consensus estimates by 5.4%. Management is guiding for a 43.6% year-on-year increase in revenue next quarter.
Looking further ahead, sell-side analysts expect revenue to grow 25.8% over the next 12 months, according to S&P, a deceleration versus the last two years. Despite the slowdown, this projection is strong and suggests the market expects success for its products and services.
The customer acquisition cost, or CAC, payback period measures the months a company needs to recoup the money spent on acquiring a new customer. This metric helps assess how quickly a business can break even on its sales and marketing investments.
AppLovin is highly efficient at acquiring new customers, and its CAC payback period was 1.2 months this quarter. The company's rapid recovery of its customer acquisition costs indicates it has a highly differentiated product offering and a strong brand reputation. These dynamics give AppLovin more resources to pursue new product initiatives while maintaining the flexibility to increase its sales and marketing investments.
AppLovin's outlook stood out in a quarter with clear positives: EBITDA guidance for next quarter came in well above analysts' consensus estimates, and revenue guidance also topped Wall Street's consensus. Shares soared 24.9% to $339.10 immediately after the results.
AppLovin had a positive quarter, but one earnings result doesn't necessarily make the stock a buy. Assessing whether it is a good investment requires considering its valuation and business quality, as well as what happened in the latest quarter. articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.
